title: Seva as spirituality
hook: service is not a side activity; it is the path

segments.voice: Yesterday, miri and piri: two swords, two buildings facing, one life. Your line was both together. What ordinary piece of work did you do with a prayer's care? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-eight.

At the door of a gurdwara, before you go in, you take off your shoes. Someone behind a counter takes them from you, slides them onto a rack, and hands you a token. When you come out, they find your pair and hand them back, sometimes wiped clean. Who is behind that counter? Nobody you hired. It could be a college student, a retired engineer, a shopkeeper on his day off, a grandmother who has done it for years. They're not paid. They're not there to be noticed. They're handling strangers' shoes, and they look content to be there. This lesson is about why that counter is not the edge of Sikh spiritual life, but close to its center.
screen: `SHOES AT THE DOOR.` → `WHO IS BEHIND THE COUNTER?` → `NOT PAID. CONTENT TO BE THERE.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Seva is selfless service: work done for others with no wage and no score kept. In a gurdwara it looks like cooking and serving in the langar, washing dishes, sweeping floors, minding shoes. Outside, it looks like anything done for someone who needs it. Second, what the Granth says. In Sri Raag, Guru Nanak puts it plainly. In paraphrase: earn service here in the world, and you'll be given a seat in the Lord's court. Notice where the service happens: in the world. Not after. Not somewhere holier. Here, at the shoe counter, at the stove. Third, a story tradition tells. During a battle, a Sikh named Bhai Ghanaiya went across the field with a water skin, giving water to the wounded, including soldiers from the other side. Some Sikhs complained to Guru Gobind Singh. Tradition says that when the Guru asked him why, Ghanaiya answered that he saw no enemy, only the Guru's face in everyone. And the Guru, tradition says, gave him ointment as well, so he could dress their wounds too. Fourth, why it's the path and not a side activity. Seva works on the very thing we met a few days ago: haumai, ego. It's hard to hold onto I, me, mine while you're scrubbing someone else's pot. So seva isn't a break from prayer. Sikhs speak of it as a form of prayer: the hands remembering what the lips say. The hope is service without the self in the way: no photo, no thank-you required. Service is the path.
screen: `SEVA: SERVICE, NO WAGE, NO SCORE.` · `EARN SERVICE HERE, IN THE WORLD.` · `BHAI GHANAIYA'S WATER SKIN.` · `HANDS THAT LOOSEN HAUMAI.` · then, large: `SERVICE IS THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve once as prayer. For the sit, settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one small act of service you could do today that nobody would ever thank you for. A dish left in the sink. A neighbor's bin. A text to someone who is struggling. Hold it in your mind. Picture doing it slowly, with care, the way someone at the shoe counter hands back a stranger's pair. Notice any part of you that wants credit for it, and let that part rest. If you pray, you can offer the act quietly with Waheguru. Then, after the bell, go and do it. The bell holds the time.
Seva as spirituality. Selfless service, done in the world, not beside the path but as the path itself. Today's word.
Your line: service is the path. Today, do one unthanked thing for someone, and don't mention it. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs do seva in gurdwaras by cooking and serving langar, washing dishes, cleaning and minding shoes, and outside them through volunteer service, understood as a spiritual practice rather than a side activity.

it also means sweeping, washing, minding shoes, and serving anyone in need.

tradition says he gave water to the wounded from both sides.

fork.setup: you're Bhai Ghanaiya on the battlefield with a water skin, and wounded men from the other side are calling for water. what do you do?
options: give water only to your own side.
give water to anyone wounded, from either side.
leave the field; it isn't your fight.
fork.reveal: tradition says he gave water to all, saw the Guru's face in everyone, and the Guru gave him ointment too.

trapdoor: what you thought: seva is volunteering, a good deed on the side.
what it means: in Sikh thought, service done without self is the path itself.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak in Sri Raag: earn service in the world, and a seat in the court is given.

notes: Editor: replaced the garbled 'not on a rota for attention'; 'earlier this week' corrected to 'a few days ago' (haumai was day 1372, the previous week); softened 'you can't really hold onto' to 'it's hard to hold onto'.
Paraphrase of 'vich dunia sev kamaaeeai, taa dargeh baisan paaeeai' (Sri Raag, Ang 26); please confirm the Ang and attribution to Guru Nanak.
The Bhai Ghanaiya story (water for the wounded of both sides, the Guru's question, the ointment) is told as tradition; please confirm the details and that no battle or place is needed.
'Sikhs speak of it as a form of prayer' is a general claim about how Sikhs understand seva; please confirm.
The hook's list of who might be at the shoe counter is illustrative, not a claim about any gurdwara.
